In NPB, a 6 man rotation with Monday as a designated off day for all teams means a starter only pitches once a week. Pitchers also like to continue throwing by the dugout between innings to stay warm.

Many NPB starters don’t prioritize velocity in the same way as their MLB counterparts, but regularly run 100+ pitch counts every start, even going 120+ pitches at times.

The pitch counts and workloads at the amateur level also go far beyond what would be accepted as normal practice in modern American youth baseball.

Yet, it’s worth noting that pitchers seemingly have fewer long-term injuries in Japan, though one could argue that teams/players are more reluctant to publicly diagnose it, pursue major surgery, etc. Some pitchers also clearly get overworked and see a dip in performance, even if they aren’t technically injured.

There are also cases where conservative treatment can sometimes delay a recovery timeline even more (e.g. Yasunobu Okugawa skipped Tommy John but still effectively missed 3 seasons; Kodai Umetsu didn’t get surgery on a major shoulder injury from 2024 for half a year and still hasn’t made a rehab start).

NPB also doesn’t have an “injured list,” so it’s not uncommon for a player to be diagnosed with something along the lines of “poor condition” and just be MIA for a few weeks or months.

But it’s relatively rare to see more than a couple of the top 50 starters in the league go down with long-term injuries any given season. 2026 is admittedly not the best example with top starters like Shunpeita Yamashita and Hiroya Miyagi both undergoing Tommy John.

It’s not because NPB teams have better medical staffs or better load management. It’s probably quite the opposite. But the truth is that many Japanese pitchers are throwing *more* and getting injured *less*.

Velocity is king, and MLB has reached a point where young players must chase it to increase their chances of success. Injuries are at an all-time high. There isn’t one solution, but 6 man rotations and more pitchers on the roster are the natural evolution.

Talk about memecoins being a "bubble about to burst" misses the main point: we are witnessing the birth of a fundamentally new economic model where the density of attention has become more valuable than any traditional product.

The financial nihilism of younger generations is not a random glitch, but a natural response to the overheated valuations of the classical market.

How this segment will transform in the future:

Memecoins as stocks of internet culture: For Gen Z and Gen Alpha, the traditional stock market with its complex reports looks stuffy and alien. Meme tokens will become their primary financial instrument — understandable, fast, and directly reflecting what the entire internet is talking about.

Fusion with streaming and SocialFi: Donations, subscriptions, and creator content will finally become tokenised. Influencers and media brands will launch not just merch, but their own meme tokens, whose market cap will react to views and reach in real time.

A hybrid of news and prediction markets: The boundary between a news hook and a financial asset will blur completely. Memecoins will turn into an interactive news feed: an event happens — the token instantly skyrockets; the agenda shifts — liquidity flows into the next trend.

Corporate brands stepping in: Large companies will have to adapt. Instead of traditional targeted advertising, corporations will start buying up and fuelling memecoins of their fans to purchase audience loyalty directly, bypassing ad agencies.

The memecoins of the future are not just short-term speculation on pictures. This is the first attempt in history to turn the pure chaos of network folklore into a full-fledged global exchange, where the currency is the most valuable thing a modern person has — their time and focus of attention.

Will Warsh Break the Hall of Mirrors?

Kevin Warsh has criticized the Federal Reserve’s forward guidance and its resulting “hall of mirrors,” where markets anticipate the Fed, the Fed watches markets, and policy becomes a validation of financial-market expectations rather than independent judgment.

Wall Street pundits have it wrong. CPI is above the Fed’s 2% target, the Bernanke handcuffs. So what? The relevant question is whether a supply shock is generating clear second- and third-order effects, a self-sustaining spread into domestic prices, wages, expectations, and excessive demand.

The data say no. Breakevens confirm. 

The clearest market signal came after the CPI release. Two-year and five-year inflation breakevens declined. The bond market’s forward-looking measure of expected inflation did not validate the claim that the report revealed a durable inflation breakout. Instead, it marked down expected inflation even as rate-hike odds rose.

That contradiction is the hall of mirrors. A backward-looking supply shock lifts CPI. Pundits demand a hike. Markets price a hike. Policymakers see the repricing and feel obliged to deliver it, even though the market’s own inflation expectations are declining.

A supply shock is already a tax on growth. Higher energy, freight, food, tariff, or input costs reduce real household income, compress business margins, and weaken spending and investment before the Fed moves.

Rate hikes do not pump more oil. They do not produce more diesel, lower tariffs, clear shipping bottlenecks, or add productive capacity. They add a second tax on growth through mortgages, business credit, capital investment, consumer durables, and housing construction.

Sound economic theory says the Fed should be still unless the supply shock is clearly spreading into persistent domestic inflation. Before hiking, it should be able to show broad domestic-services inflation, wages persistently outpacing productivity, rising medium- and long-term expectations, and robust real demand, credit, housing, and investment.
It cannot.

If the Warsh Fed yields to the hall-of-mirrors crowd, Warsh’s credibility is shot. 

A supply shock lifts CPI, pundits demand a hike, markets price it, the Fed complies, and ordinary Americans absorb the costs through weaker housing, investment, credit, and employment.

That is not credibility. It is reflex.

⚡️This is the anatomy of why people feel poorer even when the macro data says they are wealthier.

The deepest signal is not that coffee is up 123% or eggs 86%. It is that the price of participating in ordinary life has ratcheted upward across almost every gateway at once.

Shelter. Cars. Insurance. Electricity. Food. Transportation. Healthcare.

Those are not luxuries. They are the admission ticket to adulthood.

So the real economic damage is larger than “purchasing power fell.” The minimum amount of income and capital required to form a household, buy a home, raise children, commute, insure assets, and maintain a normal middle-class life has moved sharply higher.

That changes behavior.

People delay marriage.

Delay children.

Stay with parents longer.

Rent longer.

Take fewer risks.

Need two incomes where one once worked.

Become more dependent on asset appreciation just to keep pace with the denominator.

And this connects directly to demographics.

Inflation can hollow out the reproductive base of a society without ever appearing as a demographic policy.

Raise the price of shelter, healthcare, childcare, transportation, food, and energy enough, and fertility falls through economics rather than decree.

Then the age structure worsens.

Then fewer workers support more retirees.

Then fiscal pressure rises.

Then governments need more nominal growth and more debt.

Then the monetary system has even more incentive to tolerate inflation.

That is the loop.

And the cruelest part is the asset divide.

If you already owned the house, stocks, land, business, Bitcoin, gold, whatever, a large part of the inflation wave repriced your assets upward.

If you were trying to enter the system through wages alone, the ladder moved while you were climbing it.

That is why younger people can look at strong GDP, record wealth, expensive homes, booming equities and still feel like the system is getting further away.

Because aggregate wealth can rise while access to wealth collapses.

That is the deeper story in this chart.

The system did not simply make everything more expensive.

It raised the price of becoming an adult inside it.
